nuance: Can suggest irritability as well as nervousness. It does not mean physically standing near an edge.

meaning: Recovering after an illness or injury.
easyEnglish: Recovering after an illness or injury.
japanese: 病気や損傷から回復しつつある。
cue: A friend asks how you are after a cold. Give an encouraging update.
reply: I'm on the mend, though I still get tired in the afternoon.
transferCue: Your neighbor's injured dog is recovering. Share the news.
transferReply: Their dog is on the mend and taking short walks again.
frame: Be on the mend
nuance: Usually about improving health. It means recovering, not necessarily fully recovered.

phrase: on the spur of the moment
meaning: Without planning, because you suddenly decide to do something.
easyEnglish: Without planning, because you suddenly decide to do something.
japanese: 前もって考えず、その場の思いつきで。
cue: Explain why you went to a concert nobody knew you had planned.
reply: I bought the ticket on the spur of the moment after seeing the poster.
transferCue: You unexpectedly invited friends to dinner. Describe how it happened.
transferReply: We invited everyone over on the spur of the moment.
frame: Decide / do something on the spur of the moment
nuance: The expression describes spontaneity, not necessarily a reckless or bad decision.

meaning: Left with less money because you paid costs that were not covered.
easyEnglish: Left with less money because you paid costs that were not covered.
japanese: 費用を負担した結果、持ち出しや損をして。
cue: You bought supplies for an event but were not fully repaid. Explain.
reply: I'm still out of pocket after paying for the event supplies.
transferCue: A club wants volunteers to buy their own materials. Raise a concern.
transferReply: We should repay the volunteers so nobody ends up out of pocket.
frame: Be / end up out of pocket
nuance: This lesson teaches financial loss, common in UK English. Out-of-pocket costs are personal expenses; US informal out of pocket can also mean unavailable.

meaning: More extreme or elaborate than seems reasonable.
easyEnglish: More extreme or elaborate than seems reasonable.
japanese: 度が過ぎている、大げさすぎる。
cue: A friend suggests an elaborate party for a very small occasion. React gently.
reply: A private orchestra might be a bit over the top for our picnic.
transferCue: Someone reacted very dramatically to a minor mistake. Describe the reaction.
transferReply: His reaction was over the top for such a small mix-up.
frame: Something is a bit / completely over the top
nuance: Informal and evaluative. It can be critical or amused depending on tone.

meaning: Pay much more than seems reasonable.
easyEnglish: Pay much more than seems reasonable.
japanese: 法外な高値を払う。
cue: You booked a room very late during a busy festival. Describe the cost.
reply: We paid through the nose for a tiny room near the station.
transferCue: Warn a friend about buying a ticket at the last minute.
transferReply: You'll pay through the nose if you wait until the morning of the concert.
frame: Pay through the nose for something
nuance: Informal and strongly negative about the price; no literal body-related meaning is intended.

meaning: Use personal connections to get something arranged.
easyEnglish: Use personal connections to get something arranged.
japanese: 人脈を使って便宜を図る。
cue: A friend knows the venue manager and may arrange a short visit. Explain the possibility.
reply: She might be able to pull a few strings and get us a tour.
transferCue: Someone asks how you got a meeting with a busy organizer. Explain.
transferReply: My former teacher pulled a few strings to help arrange the meeting.
frame: Pull a few strings to do something
nuance: May suggest special treatment or unfair influence. It does not necessarily mean paying someone.

meaning: Make every possible effort to achieve something.
easyEnglish: Make every possible effort to achieve something.
japanese: できる限りの手を尽くす。
cue: Your team is preparing an especially important presentation. Encourage their effort.
reply: Let's pull out all the stops for this presentation.
transferCue: Your family made an unusually elaborate welcome dinner. Thank them.
transferReply: You really pulled out all the stops for dinner. Thank you!
frame: Pull out all the stops for something / to do something
nuance: Emphasizes effort and using available resources; it can describe celebrations as well as work.

meaning: Reach a conclusion by connecting pieces of information.
easyEnglish: Reach a conclusion by connecting pieces of information.
japanese: いくつかの情報を結びつけて事情を察する。
cue: You guessed a surprise visit after noticing extra bedding and food. Explain.
reply: I saw the extra bedding and put two and two together.
transferCue: A colleague worked out why the meeting had moved. Describe their reasoning.
transferReply: She put two and two together when she saw the repair team outside the room.
frame: Put two and two together and realize something
nuance: A conclusion from clues can still be wrong. It is not a claim of certainty or a literal arithmetic exercise.

meaning: Notice the mood of the people around you and respond appropriately.
easyEnglish: Notice the mood of the people around you and respond appropriately.
japanese: 周囲の雰囲気や気持ちを察して振る舞う。
cue: A friend wants to make a joke during a serious discussion. Advise them.
reply: Read the room before you make that joke; everyone looks worried.
transferCue: A presenter adjusted her tone when the audience seemed confused. Praise her awareness.
transferReply: She can read the room and knows when to slow down.
frame: Read the room before saying / doing something
nuance: Informal. A direct command can sound like criticism, so use a gentle tone when advising someone.

meaning: Finally understand or accept something you did not understand before.
easyEnglish: Finally understand or accept something you did not understand before.
japanese: それまで分からなかったことや受け入れなかったことを、ようやく理解する。
cue: A colleague finally understands why you need extra testing. Describe the change.
reply: He finally saw the light after we showed him the failures.
transferCue: You used to reject an idea but now recognize its value. Admit your change of view.
transferReply: I used to resist shared planning, but I've started to see the light.
frame: Finally / begin to see the light
nuance: Can sound self-satisfied when describing someone who now agrees with you. It differs from seeing hope at the end of a difficulty.

meaning: Available for someone to take, claim or win.
easyEnglish: Available for someone to take, claim or win.
japanese: 誰かが手に入れたり獲得したりできる状態で。
cue: You have an unused ticket and want to offer it to friends.
reply: I've got one concert ticket up for grabs if anyone wants it.
transferCue: Your club has several unfilled committee roles. Announce them.
transferReply: Two places on the committee are still up for grabs.
frame: Something is up for grabs
nuance: Informal. Availability may involve a competition, an application or simply being the first to ask.

meaning: Attract the most attention or praise at an event.
easyEnglish: Attract the most attention or praise at an event.
japanese: 主役以上に注目や称賛を集める。
cue: A child gave an unexpectedly charming performance at a family event. Describe it.
reply: Her little dance routine completely stole the show.
transferCue: A small dessert became everyone's favorite part of a dinner. Describe its success.
transferReply: The lemon tart stole the show, even though the main course took hours.
frame: Someone / something steals the show
nuance: Usually positive. Steal is figurative here and does not imply actual theft or unfair behavior.

phrase: take it with a grain of salt
meaning: Treat what you hear with some doubt rather than fully believing it.
easyEnglish: Treat what you hear with some doubt rather than fully believing it.
japanese: 聞いた話をそのまま信じず、少し疑って受け止める。
cue: A friend shares a rumor from an unreliable source. Advise caution.
reply: Take it with a grain of salt; that account often gets details wrong.
transferCue: A teammate offers an optimistic estimate without checking the figures. Suggest caution.
transferReply: I'd take it with a grain of salt until we've checked the actual costs.
frame: Take something with a grain of salt
nuance: Common in US English; a pinch of salt is common in UK English. It refers to skepticism, not ignoring all evidence.
aliases: take it with a pinch of salt

phrase: the writing is on the wall
meaning: There are clear signs that something is likely to fail or end badly.
easyEnglish: There are clear signs that something is likely to fail or end badly.
japanese: 失敗や悪い結末の兆しがはっきり見えている。
cue: A shop has lost its customers and keeps shortening its hours. Express concern.
reply: The writing is on the wall for that shop unless something changes.
transferCue: Your team has received no funding for a project that was already struggling. Assess its future.
transferReply: With the funding gone, the writing is on the wall for the project.
frame: The writing is on the wall for something
nuance: A pessimistic prediction from warning signs, not proof that an outcome is unavoidable.

meaning: Make good decisions or responses quickly in an unexpected situation.
easyEnglish: Make good decisions or responses quickly in an unexpected situation.
japanese: 予想外の状況ですばやく判断したり受け答えしたりする。
cue: A friend will host a live question session. Explain an important skill.
reply: You'll need to think on your feet when the audience asks unexpected questions.
transferCue: A teammate managed a last-minute venue change smoothly. Praise the ability involved.
transferReply: You really can think on your feet; that venue change didn't throw you.
frame: Be able to / need to think on someone's feet
nuance: About quick, useful responses under pressure, not simply thinking while standing.

meaning: Stop being careful and take a risk.
easyEnglish: Stop being careful and take a risk.
japanese: 用心するのをやめ、思い切ってリスクを取る。
cue: You accepted a spontaneous invitation to perform despite feeling nervous. Describe the decision.
reply: I threw caution to the wind and agreed to sing with the band.
transferCue: A friend wants to spend their travel budget on a sudden detour. Describe the choice.
transferReply: You could throw caution to the wind and take the detour, but check what it would cost first.
frame: Throw caution to the wind and do something
nuance: Can sound adventurous or critical. Winds is also used; the phrase does not recommend ignoring serious risks.

meaning: Good enough to meet the required standard.
easyEnglish: Good enough to meet the required standard.
japanese: 求められる水準に達している。
cue: Your first draft needs improvement before it can be shared. Assess it honestly.
reply: The draft isn't up to scratch yet, so I'll revise it before sending it.
transferCue: Your club checked old equipment before an event. Report the result.
transferReply: Most of the equipment is still up to scratch, but two microphones need replacing.
frame: Be / bring something up to scratch
nuance: Mainly UK English. Often used in the negative or when improving something to an acceptable standard.

meaning: Work very well and produce the result you wanted.
easyEnglish: Work very well and produce the result you wanted.
japanese: 期待どおりに、とてもうまくいく。
cue: A friend suggested a simple fix for a stuck drawer. Report success.
reply: That little adjustment worked like a charm; the drawer opens smoothly now.
transferCue: Your new reminder method helped you remember your keys. Describe it.
transferReply: Leaving a note on the door works like a charm for me.
frame: A method / solution works like a charm
nuance: Informal and positive. It describes a successful result, not a magical or guaranteed solution.

meaning: Freedom to decide how to do something.
easyEnglish: Freedom to decide how to do something.
japanese: やり方を自分で自由に決められること。
cue: Your manager trusts you to organize a workshop. Explain how much freedom you have.
reply: They've given me a free hand to plan the workshop, as long as we stay within budget.
transferCue: A designer asks how closely she must follow your first sketch. Reassure her.
transferReply: You have a free hand with the layout; the sketch was just a starting point.
frame: Give someone a free hand to do something
nuance: Usually follows give or have. Freedom can still exist within an agreed budget or goal.

meaning: Work you do because you enjoy or care about it, rather than for money.
easyEnglish: Work you do because you enjoy or care about it, rather than for money.
japanese: 報酬よりも、好きな気持ちや思い入れで取り組む仕事。
cue: Someone asks why you spend weekends restoring an old bicycle.
reply: It's a labor of love; I enjoy bringing each little part back to life.
transferCue: Your aunt spent months collecting family recipes. Describe her project.
transferReply: That cookbook was a labor of love, and she gave a copy to every cousin.
frame: Something is a labor of love
nuance: US spelling labor; UK labour. It can involve considerable effort even when it earns nothing.

meaning: Something you feel sure will happen sooner or later.
easyEnglish: Something you feel sure will happen sooner or later.
japanese: いずれ必ず起こると考えられること。
cue: Your friend keeps improving at chess but has not beaten you yet.
reply: It's only a matter of time before you beat me at this rate.
transferCue: A team's repeated shortcuts are starting to cause small problems. Express concern.
transferReply: If we keep skipping checks, it's a matter of time before something important goes wrong.
frame: It's only a matter of time before + clause
nuance: Expresses strong expectation, not a known schedule or a guarantee.

meaning: Fresh energy or usefulness after a change or improvement.
easyEnglish: Fresh energy or usefulness after a change or improvement.
japanese: 変化や改善によって活力や役割を取り戻すこと。
cue: An old community hall is busy again after becoming an arts center.
reply: The art classes have given that old hall a new lease of life.
transferCue: A friend seems much happier since joining a walking group.
transferReply: That walking group has given you a new lease of life; you always have a story to tell.
frame: Give someone / something a new lease of life
nuance: UK form; US English commonly uses a new lease on life. Used for people, places and objects.

meaning: A kind person whose manners are not polished.
easyEnglish: A kind person whose manners are not polished.
japanese: 言葉遣いや態度は洗練されていないが、人柄のよい人。
cue: A new volunteer sounds blunt, but always stays late to help. Describe him kindly.
reply: He's a rough diamond; his words can be blunt, but he looks after everyone.
transferCue: Your friend worries that a helpful neighbor seems a little gruff.
transferReply: She's a rough diamond, but she's the first person to help when something breaks.
frame: Someone is a rough diamond
nuance: Mainly UK in this sense. It can sound patronizing if said directly to the person.

meaning: Someone who listens and comforts you when you are upset.
easyEnglish: Someone who listens and comforts you when you are upset.
japanese: つらいときに話を聞いて慰めてくれる相手。
cue: A friend is upset and says they do not want advice right now.
reply: You don't need to explain everything; I'm here if you need a shoulder to cry on.
transferCue: Thank a cousin who listened when you had a difficult week.
transferReply: Thanks for being a shoulder to cry on when I felt so overwhelmed.
frame: Need / offer someone a shoulder to cry on
nuance: Emphasizes emotional support, not solving the problem. Actual crying is not required.

meaning: Someone or something you are very pleased to see.
easyEnglish: Someone or something you are very pleased to see.
japanese: 会えて、または目にして、とてもうれしい人やもの。
cue: A friend arrives with breakfast after you have worked an early shift.
reply: You're a sight for sore eyes, especially with that bag of warm bread.
transferCue: After a long journey, you finally see your hotel. Express relief.
transferReply: That little hotel was a sight for sore eyes after six hours on the road.
frame: Someone / something is a sight for sore eyes
nuance: An informal, warm expression of welcome or relief; it does not describe eye pain.

meaning: A lot of worry or anger about something small.
easyEnglish: A lot of worry or anger about something small.
japanese: ささいなことをめぐる大騒ぎ。
cue: A group chat argued over a typo, but everyone has now moved on.
reply: It was a storm in a teacup; the typo was fixed in a minute.
transferCue: Two clubs briefly argued about a poster color. Describe the dispute afterward.
transferReply: The poster argument turned out to be a storm in a teacup.
frame: Something is a storm in a teacup
nuance: Mainly UK; a tempest in a teapot is a US variant. Can dismiss concerns, so use with care.

phrase: a taste of things to come
meaning: An early experience that suggests what the future will be like.
easyEnglish: An early experience that suggests what the future will be like.
japanese: これから起こることを予感させる最初の体験や兆し。
cue: The first song at a concert was excellent. Describe what it suggested.
reply: That opening song was a taste of things to come; the whole concert was wonderful.
transferCue: You tried a short lesson before starting a full cooking course.
transferReply: The trial lesson gave me a taste of things to come, and now I can't wait to start.
frame: Give someone / be a taste of things to come
nuance: Can suggest either good or bad future experiences. Taste is figurative here.

meaning: A situation where one problem causes another, which makes the first worse.
easyEnglish: A situation where one problem causes another, which makes the first worse.
japanese: 問題が別の問題を生み、それが元の問題をさらに悪化させる悪循環。
cue: A team rushes because it is behind, then loses more time fixing mistakes.
reply: We're in a vicious circle: rushing creates errors, and fixing them puts us further behind.
transferCue: You avoid speaking English because you feel nervous, and the lack of practice makes you more nervous.
transferReply: I want to break this vicious circle by trying one short conversation a day.
frame: Be in / break a vicious circle
nuance: Describes problems that reinforce each other, not simply a repeated inconvenience. Vicious cycle is also common.

meaning: Honest and done according to the rules.
easyEnglish: Honest and done according to the rules.
japanese: 不正がなく、公正で正当なこと。
cue: Someone asks whether the competition judges followed the published rules.
reply: Everything was above board; the scores and judging process are available to everyone.
transferCue: You want a colleague to record an agreement openly.
transferReply: Let's put it in writing so everything stays above board.
frame: Everything is above board
nuance: Refers to honest conduct. Hyphenate above-board when it comes before a noun, as in an above-board deal.

meaning: Despite having very little chance of success.
easyEnglish: Despite having very little chance of success.
japanese: 成功の見込みがほとんどない状況にもかかわらず。
cue: A tiny local team won a tournament against much bigger clubs.
reply: Against all odds, our local team won the final.
transferCue: A neighborhood saved a library that had seemed certain to close.
transferReply: They kept the library open against all odds, with help from hundreds of neighbors.
frame: Against all odds, + clause
nuance: Emphasizes an unlikely success or survival, not just an ordinary difficulty.

meaning: A difficult or unusual task you treat as a normal part of your job.
easyEnglish: A difficult or unusual task you treat as a normal part of your job.
japanese: 大変なことや珍しいことでも、仕事のうちだと受け止めること。
cue: Someone thanks you for handling a tricky customer request. Respond lightly.
reply: It's all in a day's work, but I'm glad we found an answer for you.
transferCue: A stage manager calmly fixes a last-minute problem before a show. Describe her attitude.
transferReply: For her, solving a problem five minutes before the show is all in a day's work.
frame: It's all in a day's work
nuance: Often modest or humorous. It means routine responsibility, not that the task took a whole day.

meaning: Messy, scattered, or lacking a clear order.
easyEnglish: Messy, scattered, or lacking a clear order.
japanese: あちこちに散らばっている、または整理がつかずまとまりがない。
cue: A friend arrives while you are packing to move. Explain the mess.
reply: Sorry, my things are all over the place; I'm still sorting the boxes.
transferCue: You lost track of the order of your presentation notes.
transferReply: My notes are all over the place, so I'll rewrite them before tomorrow.
frame: Things / thoughts are all over the place
nuance: Informal. Can describe physical mess or confused organization; choose the meaning from context.

meaning: Behaving very well, especially when talking about a child.
easyEnglish: Behaving very well, especially when talking about a child.
japanese: とても行儀よくしていること。特に子どもについて使う。
cue: A parent asks whether their child behaved during the long train ride.
reply: She was as good as gold and spent most of the trip drawing.
transferCue: Your nephew stayed with you during a busy afternoon. Reassure his parent.
transferReply: He was as good as gold while I finished the work call.
frame: Someone is as good as gold
nuance: Common in UK English, usually about children. Applied to adults, it can sound patronizing.

meaning: By chance, in a way that helped or caused trouble.
easyEnglish: By chance, in a way that helped or caused trouble.
japanese: 偶然にも。都合よく、または都合悪く起きたことを述べる。
cue: You needed an umbrella and found a shop just as the rain started.
reply: As luck would have it, there was an umbrella shop beside the station.
transferCue: You finally had a free afternoon, but the museum was closed.
transferReply: As luck would have it, I picked the one day the museum was closed.
frame: As luck would have it, + clause
nuance: Can introduce good or bad luck; the rest of the sentence makes the attitude clear.

meaning: Accepting something as it appears, without looking for a hidden meaning.
easyEnglish: Accepting something as it appears, without looking for a hidden meaning.
japanese: 表面に示されたとおりに受け取り、裏の意味を考えないこと。
cue: A friend is worried that a compliment might have been sarcastic.
reply: I'd take the compliment at face value; she sounded sincere to me.
transferCue: A surprisingly cheap offer leaves out several details. Suggest caution.
transferReply: Don't take that offer at face value; ask what's included in the price.
frame: Take / accept something at face value
nuance: Often used with take. It concerns interpretation, not the physical appearance of a face.

meaning: In strong disagreement with someone.
easyEnglish: In strong disagreement with someone.
japanese: 相手と激しく対立していること。
cue: Two managers strongly disagree about where to open the next shop.
reply: The managers are at loggerheads over the new location.
transferCue: Two neighbors cannot agree on how to share a driveway.
transferReply: They've been at loggerheads about the driveway for weeks.
frame: Be at loggerheads with someone over something
nuance: Stronger than a minor difference of opinion. Usually describes an ongoing dispute.

meaning: In disagreement or not consistent with something.
easyEnglish: In disagreement or not consistent with something.
japanese: 意見が合わない、または内容が食い違っていること。
cue: A group's stated priority is rest, but it keeps scheduling late meetings.
reply: These late meetings are at odds with our promise to protect people's evenings.
transferCue: You and a friend disagree about the best route for a trip.
transferReply: We're at odds over the route, but we both want to avoid driving at night.
frame: Be at odds with someone / something
nuance: Can compare people or ideas and evidence. Less strongly confrontational than at loggerheads.

phrase: at the end of your tether
meaning: Having almost no patience or energy left to deal with a problem.
easyEnglish: Having almost no patience or energy left to deal with a problem.
japanese: 問題に対処する気力や忍耐が尽きかけていること。
cue: A friend has tried for hours to fix a printer and is getting frustrated.
reply: If you're at the end of your tether, leave it for tonight; I'll help tomorrow.
transferCue: You've dealt with repeated booking mistakes all afternoon. Explain why you need a break.
transferReply: I'm at the end of my tether after sorting out the same booking three times.
frame: Be at the end of your tether
nuance: Mainly UK; at the end of your rope is common in US English. Expresses strong frustration or exhaustion.
aliases: at the end of your rope
at the end of my tether

meaning: Lasting angry feelings between people after a past disagreement.
easyEnglish: Lasting angry feelings between people after a past disagreement.
japanese: 過去の争いが原因で残っている恨みや不仲。
cue: Two former business partners avoid each other after a difficult split.
reply: There's still bad blood between them after the business closed.
transferCue: You settled a disagreement with a teammate and want to work together again.
transferReply: I hope there's no bad blood between us; I'd like us to start fresh.
frame: Bad blood between people
nuance: Usually refers to resentment with some history, rather than a moment of irritation.

meaning: Feel an emotion so strongly that it is hard to stay calm.
easyEnglish: Feel an emotion so strongly that it is hard to stay calm.
japanese: 感情が強すぎて平静でいられない。
cue: A parent is extremely worried because their teenager has not called.
reply: I'd be beside myself with worry too; let's try calling the school.
transferCue: You were overjoyed when your sister announced a visit after years abroad.
transferReply: I was beside myself with excitement when she said she was coming home.
frame: Be beside yourself with worry / joy / excitement
nuance: Use with plus the emotion. The feeling can be positive or negative; the pronoun agrees with the subject.

meaning: In a situation you enjoy and feel comfortable handling.
easyEnglish: In a situation you enjoy and feel comfortable handling.
japanese: 得意で好きなことをして、生き生きとしている。
cue: Your friend loves explaining science and is leading a museum workshop.
reply: You're in your element here; everyone is enjoying your demonstrations.
transferCue: You feel completely at home cooking for a big group.
transferReply: I'm in my element when I have a kitchen full of people to feed.
frame: Be in your element
nuance: Describes enjoyment and a natural fit, not simply being good at a task you dislike.

meaning: Having a friendly relationship with someone.
easyEnglish: Having a friendly relationship with someone.
japanese: 相手と良好な関係にある。
cue: You left a job but still meet your former manager for coffee.
reply: I'm still on good terms with my old manager; we meet every few months.
transferCue: A friend wonders if you can ask the neighbors to collect a parcel.
transferReply: We're on good terms with the neighbors, so I'll ask if they can help.
frame: Be on good terms with someone
nuance: Terms is plural here. It refers to the relationship, not the conditions of a contract.

meaning: Thinking in similar ways and understanding each other easily.
easyEnglish: Thinking in similar ways and understanding each other easily.
japanese: 考え方や感覚が似ていて、話が通じ合う。
cue: A new teammate immediately understands the kind of design you want.
reply: We're on the same wavelength; she understood the idea from one quick sketch.
transferCue: You and a friend planned the same surprise independently.
transferReply: We must be on the same wavelength; I bought the exact same decorations.
frame: Be on the same wavelength
nuance: About shared thinking or intuition. On the same page more often emphasizes a shared understanding of a situation.

meaning: Extremely different from each other.
easyEnglish: Extremely different from each other.
japanese: 互いにまったく違う。
cue: Compare a quiet village with the busy city where you used to live.
reply: This village and my old neighborhood are worlds apart.
transferCue: Two proposed designs aim for completely different moods.
transferReply: The two designs are worlds apart; one feels playful and the other very formal.
frame: Two things are worlds apart
nuance: Usually figurative distance in character or experience, not physical distance.

meaning: Much better or greater than you ever imagined.
easyEnglish: Much better or greater than you ever imagined.
japanese: 想像していたよりもはるかにすばらしい、または規模が大きい。
cue: A small community event attracted people from across the country.
reply: The response was beyond our wildest dreams; we had to book a bigger hall.
transferCue: A friend has been offered an opportunity they never thought possible.
transferReply: That sounds beyond your wildest dreams; I remember when it was just an idea.
frame: Something is beyond your wildest dreams
nuance: An emphatic expression, often about success, opportunities or wealth. Change your to match the person.

phrase: bite the hand that feeds you
meaning: Harm or criticize someone who supports you.
easyEnglish: Harm or criticize someone who supports you.
japanese: 自分を支えてくれる相手に害を与えたり、攻撃したりする。
cue: Someone plans to mock the sponsor who funds their club. Warn them.
reply: Don't bite the hand that feeds you; raise your concerns without insulting the sponsor.
transferCue: A friend asks how to complain to someone who has helped them a lot.
transferReply: You can be honest without trying to bite the hand that feeds you.
frame: Bite the hand that feeds you
nuance: Often a warning. It can imply disloyalty, but receiving support does not make all criticism unreasonable.

meaning: Talk proudly about your own achievements.
easyEnglish: Talk proudly about your own achievements.
japanese: 自分の実績を得意げに話す、自慢する。
cue: You hesitate to describe your achievements in an interview. A friend encourages you.
reply: You don't have to blow your own trumpet, but you should explain what you contributed.
transferCue: You are pleased that a project you led received good feedback.
transferReply: I don't want to blow my own trumpet, but the feedback on my workshop was lovely.
frame: Blow your own trumpet
nuance: Mainly UK; toot your own horn is common in US English. Often used with a modest-sounding negative introduction.

meaning: Cost more money than you can comfortably afford.
easyEnglish: Cost more money than you can comfortably afford.
japanese: 無理なく払える範囲を超えるほどお金がかかる。
cue: Suggest a nice birthday meal that is still affordable.
reply: We can have a lovely dinner without breaking the bank.
transferCue: A friend wants to improve their room on a small budget.
transferReply: A few plants won't break the bank, and they'll make the room feel warmer.
frame: Something won't break the bank / without breaking the bank
nuance: Often used negatively to say something is affordable. The bank is figurative.

meaning: Contribute useful skills, ideas or resources to a group.
easyEnglish: Contribute useful skills, ideas or resources to a group.
japanese: 役立つ能力・考え・資源などを持ち寄り、貢献する。
cue: A colleague wonders what they can contribute to a new project.
reply: What you bring to the table is a deep understanding of our customers.
transferCue: Two partners have different strengths. Explain why the partnership works.
transferReply: We each bring something different to the table: I handle planning, and she knows the local market.
frame: Bring something to the table
nuance: Common in work discussions. The contribution usually goes between bring and to the table.
aliases: bring something different to the table

meaning: Very quickly and by a large amount.
easyEnglish: Very quickly and by a large amount.
japanese: 急速に、大きく進歩して。
cue: A friend has been practicing the piano regularly. Describe their progress.
reply: Your playing is improving by leaps and bounds; that piece sounds so much smoother.
transferCue: A small local shop has gained many regular customers.
transferReply: The shop has grown by leaps and bounds since the new owner took over.
frame: Improve / grow by leaps and bounds
nuance: Usually describes rapid positive progress. The order is leaps and bounds.

phrase: can't make head nor tail of
meaning: Cannot understand something at all.
easyEnglish: Cannot understand something at all.
japanese: 何が書かれているのか、何を意味するのかまったく分からない。
cue: Instructions for assembling a shelf are confusing. Ask for help.
reply: I can't make head nor tail of these diagrams; could you take a look?
transferCue: A friend sends you a message full of unfamiliar abbreviations.
transferReply: I can't make head nor tail of your message; what do those letters mean?
frame: Can't make head nor tail of something
nuance: Informal, mainly UK. US English commonly uses can't make heads or tails of.
aliases: can't make heads or tails of

meaning: Take the blame or responsibility when something goes wrong.
easyEnglish: Take the blame or responsibility when something goes wrong.
japanese: 失敗の責任や非難を引き受ける。
cue: A whole team made a decision, but only the newest member is being blamed.
reply: It isn't fair to make the newest person carry the can for a team decision.
transferCue: You approved a plan that failed. Accept responsibility.
transferReply: I signed it off, so I'll carry the can for this one.
frame: Carry the can for something / someone
nuance: Informal, mainly UK. Often suggests that the blame is being placed unfairly on one person.

meaning: Change your opinion or attitude, often very noticeably.
easyEnglish: Change your opinion or attitude, often very noticeably.
japanese: 意見や態度をがらりと変える。
cue: A friend dismissed a café until they tried its food.
reply: You might change your tune after you taste the soup.
transferCue: You opposed a later start time, but found that it helped everyone.
transferReply: I've changed my tune about the later start; the mornings feel much calmer.
frame: Change your tune about something
nuance: Often points out inconsistency and can sound teasing or critical.

meaning: Inexpensive, simple and pleasant.
easyEnglish: Inexpensive, simple and pleasant.
japanese: 安くて気軽に楽しめる、簡素だが感じのよい。
cue: Recommend a casual lunch spot to a friend on a budget.
reply: There's a cheap and cheerful noodle place around the corner.
transferCue: You want to keep a birthday gathering affordable and relaxed.
transferReply: Let's keep it cheap and cheerful: homemade pizza and a few games.
frame: A cheap and cheerful place / meal
nuance: Mainly UK and usually approving. Cheerful makes cheap sound positive rather than poor quality.

meaning: Return to a similar position or idea after a series of changes.
easyEnglish: Return to a similar position or idea after a series of changes.
japanese: いろいろな変化を経て、出発点に似た状態や考えに戻る。
cue: After trying several meeting formats, your group returns to a simple weekly chat.
reply: We've come full circle and gone back to the weekly chat we started with.
transferCue: You now teach in the room where you took your first art class.
transferReply: It feels like I've come full circle, teaching in the room where I first learned to paint.
frame: Someone / something has come full circle
nuance: A return after change or development, not necessarily a failure to make progress.

meaning: Reach a point where a problem must finally be dealt with.
easyEnglish: Reach a point where a problem must finally be dealt with.
japanese: 問題が頂点に達し、対処や決着が必要になる。
cue: A scheduling dispute can no longer be ignored before a deadline.
reply: The scheduling problem has come to a head; we need to agree on a plan today.
transferCue: Repeated noise complaints finally led to a meeting with the building manager.
transferReply: Things came to a head when three neighbors complained on the same night.
frame: A problem / situation comes to a head
nuance: Often used for tension or conflict that has been building for some time.

meaning: Start to understand and deal with something difficult.
easyEnglish: Start to understand and deal with something difficult.
japanese: 難しいことを理解し、対処し始める。
cue: You are learning a complicated booking system. Explain your progress.
reply: I'm starting to come to grips with the new booking system, but I still need the guide.
transferCue: A friend is adjusting to a major change in their daily routine.
transferReply: Give yourself time to come to grips with the new routine.
frame: Come to grips with something
nuance: US form; come to grips with also occurs in UK English, where get to grips with is common.

meaning: Not care about something at all.
easyEnglish: Not care about something at all.
japanese: まったく気にしない、どうでもよいと思う。
cue: A friend worries that you will judge their mismatched furniture.
reply: I couldn't care less if the chairs match; I'm just happy we're having dinner together.
transferCue: Someone asks whether you care who wins a TV competition.
transferReply: I couldn't care less who wins; I only watch it for the music.
frame: Couldn't care less about something / whether + clause
nuance: Informal and emphatic. It can sound dismissive, especially about another person's concern.

meaning: Unable to succeed or continue in the current situation.
easyEnglish: Unable to succeed or continue in the current situation.
japanese: 現状では成功や続行の見込みがなく、行き詰まっている。
cue: A project has lost its only source of funding. Explain the situation.
reply: Without another sponsor, the project is dead in the water.
transferCue: A proposed trip needs a permit that is no longer available.
transferReply: That route is dead in the water now that we can't get a permit.
frame: A plan / project is dead in the water
nuance: A strong negative assessment. It does not describe a small delay.

meaning: So competitive that people may harm others to succeed.
easyEnglish: So competitive that people may harm others to succeed.
japanese: 成功のためなら他人を犠牲にするほど競争が激しい。
cue: A friend asks why you left a company with intense internal competition.
reply: It felt like a dog-eat-dog environment, and I wanted a team that shared ideas.
transferCue: Two small shops help each other instead of competing aggressively.
transferReply: Business doesn't have to be dog-eat-dog; those shops do better by working together.
frame: A dog-eat-dog world / environment
nuance: Disapproving. Describes ruthless competition rather than healthy ambition.

meaning: Feeling sad and discouraged.
easyEnglish: Feeling sad and discouraged.
japanese: 落ち込んで、元気がない。
cue: A friend seems sad after a cancelled trip. Offer company.
reply: You seem a bit down in the dumps; want to go for a walk together?
transferCue: You felt disappointed after missing a family gathering.
transferReply: I was down in the dumps yesterday, but talking to my cousins helped.
frame: Be / feel down in the dumps
nuance: Informal, usually about a low mood. It is not a clinical description.

meaning: Negotiate firmly to get a deal that benefits you.
easyEnglish: Negotiate firmly to get a deal that benefits you.
japanese: 自分に有利な条件を得ようと、粘り強く交渉する。
cue: A supplier reduced the price only after a long discussion. Describe their approach.
reply: They drive a hard bargain, but we finally agreed on a price.
transferCue: A friend negotiated free delivery with a secondhand desk.
transferReply: You drive a hard bargain; I didn't expect them to include delivery too.
frame: Someone drives a hard bargain
nuance: Can express admiration or frustration. Drive is figurative and bargain is a noun here.

meaning: An unnoticed observer who can watch or hear what happens.
easyEnglish: An unnoticed observer who can watch or hear what happens.
japanese: 気づかれずにその場の様子を見聞きできる観察者。
cue: You are curious how a band chooses songs for an album.
reply: I'd love to be a fly on the wall when they choose the final songs.
transferCue: Two excellent chefs are planning a menu together. Express curiosity.
transferReply: Imagine being a fly on the wall in that kitchen while they plan the menu.
frame: Wish you could be / would love to be a fly on the wall
nuance: Usually an imagined way to observe a private conversation, not a request to participate.

meaning: Something attractive to look at but with little other value.
easyEnglish: Something attractive to look at but with little other value.
japanese: 見た目は魅力的だが、それ以上の中身や実用性が乏しいもの。
cue: A website looks beautiful but makes it hard to find basic information.
reply: The animation is eye candy, but I'd rather have a clear menu.
transferCue: A film has impressive scenery but very little story.
transferReply: It's lovely eye candy, though the story didn't hold my attention.
frame: Something is eye candy
nuance: Informal and often dismissive. Using it for a person can sound objectifying; these examples describe design and media.

meaning: Suddenly become very angry.
easyEnglish: Suddenly become very angry.
japanese: 突然かっとなる。
cue: A friend is about to respond angrily to a small mistake.
reply: Please don't fly off the handle; let's find out what happened first.
transferCue: You reacted too sharply when someone moved your things. Apologize.
transferReply: I shouldn't have flown off the handle about the boxes; you were trying to help.
frame: Fly off the handle about something
nuance: Informal and disapproving. Past flew; past participle flown.

meaning: For now, until the situation changes.
easyEnglish: For now, until the situation changes.
japanese: 状況が変わるまでの間、当面は。
cue: Your usual meeting room is being repaired. Explain the temporary arrangement.
reply: We'll use the café upstairs for the time being.
transferCue: A friend asks if you plan to replace your old phone immediately.
transferReply: I'm keeping this phone for the time being; it still does everything I need.
frame: Do something for the time being
nuance: Signals a temporary choice without specifying an end date.

meaning: Manage to speak while someone else is talking a lot.
easyEnglish: Manage to speak while someone else is talking a lot.
japanese: 相手が話し続ける中で、どうにか口を挟む。
cue: A caller talked nonstop and you could not ask a question.
reply: I couldn't get a word in edgeways, so I'll send my question by email.
transferCue: A discussion moves too quickly for a quiet teammate to join.
transferReply: Let's pause so everyone can get a word in edgeways.
frame: Can / can't get a word in edgeways
nuance: Often negative. US English commonly uses edgewise instead of edgeways.

phrase: get off on the wrong foot
meaning: Begin a relationship or activity badly.
easyEnglish: Begin a relationship or activity badly.
japanese: 関係や物事の出だしでつまずく。
cue: You arrived late to your first meeting with a new team and want to apologize.
reply: I don't want to get off on the wrong foot; I'm sorry I kept you waiting.
transferCue: You and a new neighbor misunderstood each other at first.
transferReply: We got off on the wrong foot, but we've become good friends since then.
frame: Get off on the wrong foot with someone
nuance: Often about a poor first impression that can still be repaired.

phrase: give the benefit of the doubt
meaning: Choose to believe someone when you are not sure what happened.
easyEnglish: Choose to believe someone when you are not sure what happened.
japanese: 真相がはっきりしないとき、ひとまず相手を信じる。
cue: A teammate missed a message and says their phone was broken.
reply: Let's give her the benefit of the doubt and ask when she can reply.
transferCue: A friend thinks a short email was intentionally rude. Suggest a kinder reading.
transferReply: I'd give him the benefit of the doubt; he may have written it in a hurry.
frame: Give someone the benefit of the doubt
nuance: The person comes after give. It is a provisional, favorable judgment rather than proof.
aliases: give her the benefit of the doubt
give him the benefit of the doubt
give someone the benefit of the doubt

meaning: Become more and more successful.
easyEnglish: Become more and more successful.
japanese: ますます順調になり、成功を重ねる。
cue: A friend's small bakery has gained loyal customers and added a class.
reply: Your bakery seems to go from strength to strength; the classes look really popular.
transferCue: A local reading group has steadily grown over several years.
transferReply: The group has gone from strength to strength since it found a regular venue.
frame: Someone / something goes from strength to strength
nuance: Positive and often used for continued success over time, rather than one lucky result.

meaning: Be closely connected and often happen together.
easyEnglish: Be closely connected and often happen together.
japanese: 密接に結びついていて、一緒に進む。
cue: Explain why a team needs both clear goals and room to experiment.
reply: Clear goals and creative freedom can go hand in hand.
transferCue: A friend thinks speaking practice and listening practice are unrelated.
transferReply: Listening and speaking go hand in hand; each gives you something to use in the other.
frame: Something goes hand in hand with something else
nuance: Describes a close connection. It does not by itself prove that one thing causes the other.

meaning: Go wrong or fail, especially when talking about a plan.
easyEnglish: Go wrong or fail, especially when talking about a plan.
japanese: 計画などがうまくいかなくなる。
cue: A picnic plan might fail if the weather changes. Suggest a backup.
reply: If the weather goes pear-shaped, we can have lunch at my place.
transferCue: Your weekend plans fell apart after a train cancellation.
transferReply: The whole plan went pear-shaped when the last train was cancelled.
frame: A plan / situation goes pear-shaped
nuance: Informal, mainly UK. Often used with humor about things going wrong.

meaning: Feel a special liking or affection for someone or something.
easyEnglish: Feel a special liking or affection for someone or something.
japanese: 人やものに特別な愛着がある。
cue: A friend asks why you always visit the same old bookshop.
reply: I have a soft spot for that shop; it's where I bought my first novel in English.
transferCue: You enjoy helping beginners because you remember your own first day.
transferReply: I have a soft spot for new members who are nervous about joining in.
frame: Have a soft spot for someone / something
nuance: Warm and personal. Does not mean that someone is weak or easily damaged.

meaning: Have the authority to make the final decision.
easyEnglish: Have the authority to make the final decision.
japanese: 最終的に決める権限を持つ。
cue: Several people can suggest a poster design, but one person must approve it.
reply: Everyone can suggest changes, but the organizer will have the final say.
transferCue: You are helping a friend choose furniture for their own room.
transferReply: I'll help compare the options, but you have the final say; it's your room.
frame: Have the final say on / in something
nuance: Refers to decision-making authority here, not simply speaking last in an argument.

meaning: Stuck doing the same things in a way that has become boring.
easyEnglish: Stuck doing the same things in a way that has become boring.
japanese: 同じことの繰り返しで、退屈な状態から抜け出せない。
cue: Your evenings all feel the same. Explain why you joined a class.
reply: I felt stuck in a rut, so I signed up for a pottery class.
transferCue: A team keeps repeating the same tired event format.
transferReply: We're in a rut with these events; let's ask members what they'd enjoy.
frame: Be / feel stuck in a rut
nuance: Describes an unsatisfying routine, not every regular habit.

phrase: in a league of your own
meaning: Much better at something than everyone else being compared.
easyEnglish: Much better at something than everyone else being compared.
japanese: 比べられるほかの人よりも、実力がずば抜けている。
cue: A friend made an exceptionally detailed model for an exhibition.
reply: You're in a league of your own when it comes to those tiny details.
transferCue: One local bakery makes pastries far better than the others you have tried.
transferReply: That bakery is in a league of its own; even the plain rolls are wonderful.
frame: Be in a league of your own
nuance: Strong praise that implies superiority. Change the possessive to fit the subject.
aliases: in a league of its own

meaning: In an awkward or difficult situation.
easyEnglish: In an awkward or difficult situation.
japanese: 困った、やっかいな状況にある。
cue: You locked your keys inside and your spare is with a friend who is away.
reply: I'm in a pickle: my keys are inside, and the spare is across town.
transferCue: A friend promised to help at two events at the same time.
transferReply: You're in a bit of a pickle; could someone cover one of the events?
frame: Be in a pickle
nuance: Informal and often lighthearted. Better suited to everyday predicaments than very serious harm.
aliases: in a bit of a pickle

meaning: In an extremely short moment.
easyEnglish: In an extremely short moment.
japanese: ほんの一瞬で。
cue: You looked away and a playful dog grabbed a sandwich.
reply: The dog grabbed the sandwich in a split second.
transferCue: You recognized an old classmate as soon as they entered the room.
transferReply: I knew who she was in a split second, even after all those years.
frame: Something happens in a split second
nuance: Emphasizes suddenness or speed. Split-second is hyphenated before a noun, as in a split-second decision.

meaning: Very soon or very quickly.
easyEnglish: Very soon or very quickly.
japanese: すぐに、あっという間に。
cue: A friend worries that a small packing task will take all afternoon.
reply: With both of us helping, we'll finish in no time.
transferCue: Your new neighbor learned the bus route very quickly.
transferReply: She knew the route in no time and was showing me shortcuts by Friday.
frame: Do something / be somewhere in no time
nuance: Informal reassurance or emphasis; it does not literally mean zero time.

meaning: In trouble with someone because they are annoyed with you.
easyEnglish: In trouble with someone because they are annoyed with you.
japanese: 相手を怒らせて、機嫌を損ねている状態。
cue: You forgot to return a friend's favorite book again.
reply: I'm in the doghouse for forgetting that book again; I'll take it over tonight.
transferCue: A brother ate the last piece of cake that had been saved for someone else.
transferReply: He's in the doghouse with his sister over that last slice of cake.
frame: Be in the doghouse with someone for / over something
nuance: Informal and often humorous. Usually describes personal disapproval, not a formal punishment.

meaning: Owing money or spending more money than is coming in.
easyEnglish: Owing money or spending more money than is coming in.
japanese: 赤字である、収入より支出が多い。
cue: A club spent more on an event than it received in ticket sales.
reply: The club is in the red after the event, so we're reviewing the costs.
transferCue: A shop owner explains why they are reducing some expenses.
transferReply: We've been in the red for two months, and we need to cut unnecessary costs.
frame: Be / go in the red
nuance: An accounting metaphor used in everyday discussion. In the black is the opposite.

meaning: Deeply involved in the busiest or most active part of something.
easyEnglish: Deeply involved in the busiest or most active part of something.
japanese: 物事が最も忙しく動いている、その真っただ中にいる。
cue: You cannot take a long call while preparing a large event.
reply: I'm in the thick of setting up the exhibition; can I call you this evening?
transferCue: Your friends are halfway through a complicated house move.
transferReply: They're in the thick of the move, so I'll drop off dinner rather than stay for a visit.
frame: Be in the thick of something / doing something
nuance: Can describe busy activity or a dangerous situation. Here it means active involvement.

meaning: In the same situation as another person.
easyEnglish: In the same situation as another person.
japanese: 相手と同じ立場にいるとしたら。
cue: A friend is unsure whether to ask for an extension. Offer your perspective.
reply: If I were in your shoes, I'd ask today and explain what is still left to do.
transferCue: Someone asks how you would handle a noisy neighbor.
transferReply: I can't decide for you, but in your shoes I'd start with a friendly conversation.
frame: If I were in your shoes, I'd…
nuance: Often introduces advice while imagining another person's position. It does not guarantee you understand every detail.

meaning: Prevented from getting closer or causing trouble.
easyEnglish: Prevented from getting closer or causing trouble.
japanese: 近づいたり悪影響を及ぼしたりしないよう、抑えられている。
cue: You are hungry, but dinner is not ready. Explain why you are having a small snack.
reply: A few crackers should keep my hunger at bay until dinner.
transferCue: You turn off alerts while reading to avoid distractions.
transferReply: Keeping my phone in another room helps hold distractions at bay.
frame: Keep / hold someone or something at bay
nuance: Usually used with keep or hold. Can refer to physical threats or unwanted feelings and distractions.

meaning: In complete detail, when talking about knowing something.
easyEnglish: In complete detail, when talking about knowing something.
japanese: 知識について使うと、隅々まで、知り尽くして。
cue: A friend needs advice from someone who knows the neighborhood extremely well.
reply: Ask Maya; she knows this neighborhood inside out.
transferCue: You have used a camera for years and know every setting.
transferReply: I know this camera inside out, so I don't need to check the manual often.
frame: Know / understand something inside out
nuance: This lesson teaches detailed knowledge. Clothing can also be inside out, meaning the inner side faces outward.

phrase: leave a lot to be desired
meaning: Be much less good than expected or wanted.
easyEnglish: Be much less good than expected or wanted.
japanese: 期待される水準に達しておらず、改善の余地が大きい。
cue: A hotel had a lovely view but poor service. Give balanced feedback.
reply: The view was wonderful, but the service left a lot to be desired.
transferCue: A first draft contains useful ideas but is hard to follow.
transferReply: The ideas are promising, though the structure leaves a lot to be desired.
frame: Something leaves a lot to be desired
nuance: An indirect but fairly strong criticism. Not the same as saying there are only a few small improvements to make.

meaning: Relax and enjoy yourself more freely than usual.
easyEnglish: Relax and enjoy yourself more freely than usual.
japanese: 普段の緊張を解いて、のびのび楽しむ。
cue: A friend has finished a demanding project. Suggest a relaxed evening.
reply: You've finished the project; come over and let your hair down for a while.
transferCue: You enjoyed a casual party after a week of formal events.
transferReply: It was nice to let my hair down and laugh with old friends.
frame: Let your hair down
nuance: Informal. Actual hairstyle and drinking alcohol are not part of the meaning.

meaning: Repeating the same words or request too often.
easyEnglish: Repeating the same words or request too often.
japanese: 同じ話や頼みごとを何度も繰り返して。
cue: You need to remind the group again to label shared food.
reply: I know I sound like a broken record, but please label anything you put in the fridge.
transferCue: You keep giving the same advice to a friend. Acknowledge the repetition.
transferReply: I'm starting to sound like a broken record, so I'll stop repeating myself.
frame: Sound like a broken record
nuance: Usually critical or self-deprecating. The image is an old record replaying the same short section.

meaning: Completely different in character or preferences.
easyEnglish: Completely different in character or preferences.
japanese: 性格や好みがまるで違う。
cue: Two siblings have very different personalities.
reply: Those two are like chalk and cheese: one loves crowds, and the other likes quiet evenings.
transferCue: You and a close friend enjoy entirely different holidays.
transferReply: We're like chalk and cheese when it comes to holidays, but we still enjoy each other's company.
frame: Two people are like chalk and cheese
nuance: Mainly UK. Difference does not necessarily imply dislike or conflict.

meaning: Lose other people's respect or feel publicly embarrassed.
easyEnglish: Lose other people's respect or feel publicly embarrassed.
japanese: 面目を失う、人前で恥をかいて評価を落とす。
cue: A manager is afraid that admitting a small mistake will weaken their reputation.
reply: You won't lose face by admitting the mistake; people will appreciate your honesty.
transferCue: You want to correct a friend without embarrassing them in front of everyone.
transferReply: Let's talk privately so nobody has to lose face.
frame: Someone loses face
nuance: Often about social standing in front of others. Save face means avoid that loss of respect.

meaning: End a relationship or connection completely.
easyEnglish: End a relationship or connection completely.
japanese: 関係やつながりをきっぱり断つ。
cue: You want to leave a stressful volunteer role without continuing to manage it from afar.
reply: I need to make a clean break and let the new coordinator take over.
transferCue: A friend keeps accepting tasks from a job they have already left.
transferReply: If you want to make a clean break, you'll need to tell them you're no longer available.
frame: Make a clean break with / from something
nuance: Emphasizes a definite ending, not a short rest. It need not involve a hostile departure.

meaning: Become known and respected for what you do.
easyEnglish: Become known and respected for what you do.
japanese: 実績によって名を知られ、評価されるようになる。
cue: A friend is starting to build a reputation as a photographer.
reply: You can make a name for yourself with work like this; those portraits are excellent.
transferCue: A local cook became well known for simple seasonal meals.
transferReply: She made a name for herself by turning local vegetables into memorable dishes.
frame: Make a name for yourself as + role / by doing something
nuance: Usually about recognition within a field or community, not necessarily worldwide fame.

meaning: Decide what you want to do or choose.
easyEnglish: Decide what you want to do or choose.
japanese: どうするか、何を選ぶかを決める。
cue: A friend feels rushed to choose between two courses.
reply: You don't have to make up your mind today; the deadline is next week.
transferCue: You have finally chosen where to spend a short holiday.
transferReply: I've made up my mind: I'm going to spend the weekend by the sea.
frame: Make up your mind about something / to do something
nuance: The possessive follows the person deciding. Said as a command, it can sound impatient.

meaning: More detail or complexity than is obvious at first.
easyEnglish: More detail or complexity than is obvious at first.
japanese: 一見しただけでは分からない事情や複雑さがある。
cue: A repair looks simple, but several hidden parts are involved.
reply: There's more than meets the eye here; we need to inspect the inside before estimating the cost.
transferCue: A quiet local festival has a long and complicated history.
transferReply: There's more than meets the eye to this festival; every decoration tells part of its history.
frame: There's more than meets the eye to something
nuance: Suggests hidden complexity or meaning, not necessarily dishonesty.

phrase: not the end of the world
meaning: Disappointing, but not as serious as it may feel.
easyEnglish: Disappointing, but not as serious as it may feel.
japanese: 残念ではあっても、取り返しのつかないほどのことではない。
cue: A friend is upset because they missed a casual club meeting.
reply: It's not the end of the world; they'll be happy to see you next week.
transferCue: You broke a mug while washing up and feel embarrassed.
transferReply: It's not the end of the world, but I'm sorry about the mug; I'll replace it.
frame: It's not the end of the world if + clause
nuance: Usually reassurance about a manageable setback. Can sound dismissive when someone is deeply upset.

meaning: Not intended to be publicly reported or officially recorded.
easyEnglish: Not intended to be publicly reported or officially recorded.
japanese: 公表や公式な記録をしないことを前提に。
cue: You want to share a personal opinion without it appearing in meeting minutes.
reply: Can I say something off the record before we write the summary?
transferCue: A reporter asks to quote a casual remark that you had agreed was private.
transferReply: That comment was off the record; please don't include it in the article.
frame: Say / speak off the record
nuance: Agree on this before sharing information. The phrase alone does not make a conversation confidential.

meaning: In a tense situation where the result is very uncertain.
easyEnglish: In a tense situation where the result is very uncertain.
japanese: 結果がどうなるか分からず、緊張した際どい状況にある。
cue: An outdoor concert depends on a weather forecast that keeps changing.
reply: The concert is on a knife-edge until we get the final weather update.
transferCue: A close vote will decide whether a community venue stays open.
transferReply: The future of the venue is on a knife-edge, with only one vote between the two sides.
frame: Something is on a knife-edge
nuance: Emphasizes both uncertainty and tension, often where a small change could decide the result.

meaning: Busy and active, often moving from one task or place to another.
easyEnglish: Busy and active, often moving from one task or place to another.
japanese: 忙しく動き回っている。
cue: You have been running errands since early morning. Explain why you want a quiet evening.
reply: I've been on the go since seven, so I'd love a quiet evening at home.
transferCue: A friend is constantly organizing activities during a holiday.
transferReply: You're always on the go; shall we leave one afternoon completely free?
frame: Be on the go
nuance: This lesson teaches being busy. The phrase can also mean while travelling, as in breakfast on the go.

meaning: Given free by a restaurant, café or other business.
easyEnglish: Given free by a restaurant, café or other business.
japanese: 店から無料で提供される、サービスで出される。
cue: A café kept you waiting and offers a free coffee. Explain the gesture to a friend.
reply: The coffee is on the house because we had to wait so long.
transferCue: You work at a restaurant and want to offer a complimentary dessert.
transferReply: Dessert is on the house tonight; thanks for celebrating with us.
frame: Something is on the house
nuance: The business pays. If you personally pay for a friend's meal, say it's on me instead.

meaning: Feeling a little unhappy or not quite yourself.
easyEnglish: Feeling a little unhappy or not quite yourself.
japanese: なんとなく気分がすぐれず、いつもの調子が出ない。
cue: A friend notices that you are unusually quiet today.
reply: I'm a bit out of sorts today; I think I just need a quiet evening.
transferCue: Your brother has seemed unsettled since returning from a long trip.
transferReply: He's been out of sorts since he got back, so we're giving him some space.
frame: Be / feel out of sorts
nuance: Usually mild and vague. It can include feeling slightly unwell as well as being in a low mood.

meaning: In a position where someone can make you accept their terms.
easyEnglish: In a position where someone can make you accept their terms.
japanese: 相手の条件を受け入れざるを得ない、弱い立場にある。
cue: A venue knows you have no alternative and raises its price at the last minute.
reply: They've got us over a barrel; every other venue is booked.
transferCue: You want to arrange a backup supplier before renewing a contract.
transferReply: Let's find another supplier so this one doesn't have us over a barrel.
frame: Have / get someone over a barrel
nuance: Informal. Emphasizes unequal bargaining power or a lack of real choice.

meaning: Do your fair share of a group's work.
easyEnglish: Do your fair share of a group's work.
japanese: 共同作業で自分の分の役割を果たす。
cue: You want everyone to help prepare a shared dinner.
reply: We all need to pull our weight; I'll cook if someone else handles the washing-up.
transferCue: You have just joined a volunteer group and want to help properly.
transferReply: I want to pull my weight, so please give me a regular task.
frame: Pull your weight
nuance: About a fair contribution, not necessarily doing identical tasks or hours. A direct accusation can sound harsh.

meaning: Act as if you are not worried or upset by something.
easyEnglish: Act as if you are not worried or upset by something.
japanese: 心配や落胆を表に出さず、気丈に振る舞う。
cue: A friend jokes after a disappointment, but you know they are upset.
reply: You don't have to put a brave face on it with me; I'm happy to listen.
transferCue: You tried to seem cheerful when an event you organized was cancelled.
transferReply: I put a brave face on the cancellation, but I was really disappointed.
frame: Put a brave face on something
nuance: Describes outward behavior despite difficult feelings; it does not mean the problem has been solved.

phrase: put your money where your mouth is
meaning: Support what you say with real action or resources.
easyEnglish: Support what you say with real action or resources.
japanese: 口で言うだけでなく、行動や資源を出して示す。
cue: A friend says the community garden matters but has not helped yet. Challenge them lightly.
reply: Here's a chance to put your money where your mouth is: join us at the garden on Saturday.
transferCue: You publicly supported a local project and now want to contribute.
transferReply: I'll put my money where my mouth is and volunteer for the first cleanup.
frame: Put your money where your mouth is
nuance: Often a challenge to act. The action can involve time or effort rather than literal money.
aliases: put my money where my mouth is

meaning: Spoil someone's enjoyment or enthusiasm.
easyEnglish: Spoil someone's enjoyment or enthusiasm.
japanese: 相手の喜びや盛り上がりに水を差す。
cue: A friend is excited about a picnic, but you need to mention a practical problem.
reply: I don't want to rain on your parade, but the park closes at six.
transferCue: Someone doubts a project you are enjoying. Keep your enthusiasm.
transferReply: I'm still excited about it, and I won't let one doubtful comment rain on my parade.
frame: Rain on someone's parade
nuance: Informal. Often softened with I don't want to before unwelcome information.

meaning: Exactly suited to your interests or skills.
easyEnglish: Exactly suited to your interests or skills.
japanese: 好みや得意分野にぴったり合っている。
cue: Recommend a puzzle café to a friend who loves board games.
reply: This café sounds right up your alley; every table has a different puzzle.
transferCue: A friend offers you a project involving maps and local history.
transferReply: That's right up my alley; I love maps and neighborhood stories.
frame: Something is right up your alley
nuance: Informal, especially US. Right up your street is a common UK equivalent.

meaning: At a very high level, or rising very sharply.
easyEnglish: At a very high level, or rising very sharply.
japanese: 非常に高い水準に達して、または急激に上がって。
cue: Tickets became extremely expensive after a concert announcement.
reply: Ticket prices have gone through the roof since the new dates were announced.
transferCue: A small shop received far more orders than usual after a local article.
transferReply: Orders went through the roof after the article came out.
frame: Prices / demand / numbers go through the roof
nuance: This lesson teaches a sharp rise. A person going through the roof can instead mean becoming very angry.

meaning: Suspect that something dishonest or wrong is happening.
easyEnglish: Suspect that something dishonest or wrong is happening.
japanese: 何か不正やおかしなことがあると勘づく。
cue: An unfamiliar seller asks you to pay outside the usual checkout page.
reply: I smell a rat; why won't they let us use the normal payment page?
transferCue: A story kept changing every time you asked for details.
transferReply: I began to smell a rat when the details changed for the third time.
frame: Smell a rat
nuance: Informal. Expresses suspicion, not confirmed proof that someone has done something wrong.

meaning: Someone who looks almost exactly like another person.
easyEnglish: Someone who looks almost exactly like another person.
japanese: 別の人と見た目がそっくりな人、生き写し。
cue: You see a childhood photo of your friend's mother.
reply: You're the spitting image of your mother in that photo.
transferCue: A cousin's baby looks remarkably like their grandfather.
transferReply: That baby is the spitting image of his grandfather, especially when he smiles.
frame: Be the spitting image of someone
nuance: Usually with the and of. It refers to appearance, not necessarily personality.

meaning: Keep your position or decision despite pressure to change it.
easyEnglish: Keep your position or decision despite pressure to change it.
japanese: 反対や圧力があっても、自分の意見や決定を貫く。
cue: A friend chose a smaller wedding and is being pressured to expand it.
reply: If a small wedding matters to you, stick to your guns and explain why.
transferCue: You kept a reasonable project deadline even when people asked you to rush.
transferReply: I stuck to my guns about the deadline, and we had time to check everything properly.
frame: Stick to your guns about / on something
nuance: Often positive about firmness, but context can suggest stubbornness. The image is figurative.

meaning: Hide or ignore a problem instead of dealing with it.
easyEnglish: Hide or ignore a problem instead of dealing with it.
japanese: 問題を解決せず、隠したり見て見ぬふりをしたりする。
cue: A team wants to ignore repeated complaints because they are inconvenient.
reply: We can't sweep these complaints under the carpet; we need to understand what's going wrong.
transferCue: You want a mistake discussed openly during a project review.
transferReply: Let's not sweep it under the carpet; talking about it could prevent the same mistake.
frame: Sweep something under the carpet
nuance: Mainly UK wording; under the rug is common in US English. The object normally follows sweep.
aliases: sweep these complaints under the carpet

phrase: take a leaf out of your book
meaning: Copy a useful habit or approach from someone else.
easyEnglish: Copy a useful habit or approach from someone else.
japanese: 相手のよい習慣ややり方を見習う。
cue: A friend always prepares lunch the night before and has calmer mornings.
reply: I should take a leaf out of your book and make lunch the night before.
transferCue: You admire how a colleague keeps clear notes after each meeting.
transferReply: I'd like to take a leaf out of your book; those short summaries make everything easier.
frame: Take a leaf out of someone's book
nuance: Means follow a good example. Leaf means a page here; it is not usually about copying a whole work.

phrase: the early bird catches the worm
meaning: People who act early have a better chance of getting what they want.
easyEnglish: People who act early have a better chance of getting what they want.
japanese: 早く行動する人ほど、よい機会を得やすい。
cue: A popular workshop has limited places. Encourage your friend to book early.
reply: The early bird catches the worm; let's book before all the places are gone.
transferCue: You arrived at a market early and found the best choice of fruit.
transferReply: The early bird catches the worm; we had the whole fruit stall to choose from.
frame: The early bird catches the worm
nuance: A proverb about acting before others. It can refer to quick action, not only getting up early.

meaning: The detailed and sometimes complicated parts of something.
easyEnglish: The detailed and sometimes complicated parts of something.
japanese: 物事の詳しい仕組みや細かな事情。
cue: You need someone to explain how a community club is organized.
reply: Could you show me the ins and outs of how the club runs?
transferCue: A coworker knows every detail of the room booking process.
transferReply: Ask Ravi; he knows the ins and outs of the booking system.
frame: Know / explain the ins and outs of something
nuance: Ins and outs stays plural. Often used for practical knowledge of a process.

meaning: The largest part of something.
easyEnglish: The largest part of something.
japanese: 全体のうち最も大きな取り分や割合。
cue: One teammate did most of the preparation for an event. Give them credit.
reply: Nina did the lion's share of the preparation, so she deserves a special thank-you.
transferCue: Most of a renovation budget went toward fixing the roof.
transferReply: The roof took the lion's share of the budget, leaving little for decoration.
frame: Do / receive / take the lion's share of something
nuance: Means the largest portion, often most of the total. It does not imply that the division is fair.

meaning: Get married.
easyEnglish: Get married.
japanese: 結婚する。
cue: A friend asks whether your cousins have chosen a wedding date.
reply: They're going to tie the knot next spring, in a small ceremony by the sea.
transferCue: You meet a couple who recently got married.
transferReply: Congratulations! I heard you tied the knot last month.
frame: Two people tie the knot
nuance: Informal and usually cheerful. Refers to marriage, not just moving in together.

meaning: Living or staying in the same building.
easyEnglish: Living or staying in the same building.
japanese: ひとつ屋根の下で暮らす、同じ建物にいる。
cue: Several generations of your family are staying together for a holiday.
reply: It's lovely having everyone under the same roof for a few days.
transferCue: You and a friend are considering sharing a house. Discuss expectations.
transferReply: Before we live under the same roof, let's talk about chores and quiet hours.
frame: Live / stay under the same roof
nuance: Can describe family, housemates or organizations sharing a building; it does not imply a romantic relationship.

meaning: Deliberately stop being involved in or responsible for something.
easyEnglish: Deliberately stop being involved in or responsible for something.
japanese: 関与や責任を持つのをやめ、きっぱり手を引く。
cue: A teammate wants to stop dealing with a problem they helped create.
reply: You can't just wash your hands of the problem; the rest of us still need your help.
transferCue: You have repeatedly helped organize an event, but the same agreements keep being ignored.
transferReply: I'm ready to wash my hands of this event if our agreements keep being ignored.
frame: Wash your hands of someone / something
nuance: A strong expression of withdrawal. It can sound critical when someone is avoiding responsibility.

meaning: A request that will be difficult to fulfill.
easyEnglish: A request that will be difficult to fulfill.
japanese: 相手にとって負担の大きい依頼。
cue: You need a colleague to review a long report by tomorrow. Acknowledge the effort.
reply: I know it's a big ask, but could you review the report by tomorrow?
transferCue: A friend wants everyone to travel overnight for a short party. Respond gently.
transferReply: That's a big ask for people who have work the next morning.
frame: Be a big ask / I know it's a big ask
nuance: Informal. Recognizes that a request is demanding; it does not by itself make the request reasonable.

meaning: An upsetting fact or result that you have to accept.
easyEnglish: An upsetting fact or result that you have to accept.
japanese: つらくても受け入れなければならない現実。
cue: Your project lost funding after months of work. Describe your reaction.
reply: The cancellation was a bitter pill to swallow after all that work.
transferCue: A friend asks how you feel about missing a place on a course.
transferReply: It's a bitter pill to swallow, but I can apply again next year.
frame: Be a bitter pill to swallow
nuance: Use the whole phrase for an unwelcome reality, not literal medicine. The shorter a bitter pill is also common.

meaning: A chance to start again without past mistakes counting against you.
easyEnglish: A chance to start again without past mistakes counting against you.
japanese: 過去の失敗や問題を引きずらず、やり直せる状態。
cue: You and a friend have resolved an old disagreement. Suggest a fresh start.
reply: Let's begin with a clean slate and agree on what works for both of us.
transferCue: Describe how a new teacher treated students who had struggled before.
transferReply: She gave everyone a clean slate at the start of the term.
frame: Start with a clean slate / give someone a clean slate
nuance: The metaphor is an erased writing surface. It concerns a fresh start, not erasing obligations without agreement.

meaning: Someone whose abilities or interests turn out to be surprising.
easyEnglish: Someone whose abilities or interests turn out to be surprising.
japanese: 意外な才能や一面を持つ人。
cue: A quiet colleague performs brilliantly at a music night. React warmly.
reply: You're a dark horse! I had no idea you played the violin.
transferCue: Tell a friend about an unexpected skill your neighbor has.
transferReply: He's a dark horse; he used to design sets for the theater.
frame: Someone is a dark horse
nuance: This lesson uses the hidden-talent sense. In a competition, a dark horse can also be an unexpected potential winner.

meaning: An achievement that gives you a reason to feel proud.
easyEnglish: An achievement that gives you a reason to feel proud.
japanese: 誇りにできる実績。
cue: A small team wins a respected design award. Congratulate them.
reply: That award is a feather in your cap.
transferCue: Describe what hosting an international event means for your town.
transferReply: Getting the festival here is a feather in our cap.
frame: Be a feather in someone's cap
nuance: Change the possessive to match the person or group. Usually about recognition or an achievement, not ordinary luck.

meaning: A small but important difference between two similar things.
easyEnglish: A small but important difference between two similar things.
japanese: 似ている二つのことの、わずかだが重要な違い。
cue: Your friend wants to help someone but worries about interfering.
reply: There's a fine line between offering help and taking over.
transferCue: Discuss humor in a work presentation.
transferReply: We need to watch the fine line between being playful and being rude.
frame: A fine line between A and B
nuance: Often contrasts acceptable and unacceptable behavior. Between needs two sides, whether named directly or clear from context.

meaning: A success that happens briefly and is not repeated.
easyEnglish: A success that happens briefly and is not repeated.
japanese: 一時的な成功で終わるもの。
cue: Your first video became popular. Explain why you want to keep improving.
reply: I don't want that first video to be a flash in the pan.
transferCue: A friend doubts a new restaurant will remain popular. Respond.
transferReply: It may be more than a flash in the pan; the regular customers keep returning.
frame: Be a flash in the pan
nuance: Often used about early success that does not last. Calling someone this directly can sound dismissive.

meaning: A result that seems certain before it happens.
easyEnglish: A result that seems certain before it happens.
japanese: 起こる前から明らかだと思われる結果。
cue: People assume a well-known team will win. Remind them it is not settled.
reply: Their victory isn't a foregone conclusion; the other team has improved.
transferCue: Explain why a selection process felt pointless.
transferReply: Everyone acted as if the appointment was a foregone conclusion.
frame: Be a foregone conclusion / not a foregone conclusion
nuance: Fairly formal. Describes perceived certainty; the result need not actually be guaranteed.

meaning: Someone who joins in or accepts losing without complaining.
easyEnglish: Someone who joins in or accepts losing without complaining.
japanese: 負けたり面倒なことがあったりしても、気持ちよく応じる人。
cue: Your friend cheerfully joins an unfamiliar party game. Thank them.
reply: Thanks for being a good sport about the game.
transferCue: Describe a player who congratulated the winner after a close match.
transferReply: She was a good sport and stayed to cheer at the prize ceremony.
frame: Be a good sport / be a good sport about something
nuance: Informal in American English and sometimes old-fashioned in British English. Be a good sport can sound pressuring when used to demand a favor.

meaning: Someone whose unpredictable actions may cause trouble for others.
easyEnglish: Someone whose unpredictable actions may cause trouble for others.
japanese: 予測できない言動で周りに問題を起こしかねない人。
cue: A teammate promises things to clients without checking. Describe your concern privately.
reply: He's becoming a loose cannon with these promises about delivery dates.
transferCue: Explain why an organizer was not allowed to speak for the group.
transferReply: They saw her as a loose cannon after she announced an unapproved plan.
frame: Be a loose cannon / see someone as a loose cannon
nuance: A strong, disapproving label. Describe specific behavior rather than casually using it to judge someone's character.

meaning: A choice that seems easy because the best option is obvious.
easyEnglish: A choice that seems easy because the best option is obvious.
japanese: ほとんど迷う必要のない選択。
